procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 16.10.2023 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in CRLMC No. 6066 of 2019
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Delhi refused to quash FIR No. 272 of 2019 dated 29.09.2019 registered with Police Station South Rohini, Delhi under Sections 376(2)(n) and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (“IPC” for short). The application was filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (“CrPC” for short).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, being aggrieved by the High Court's order refusing to quash the FIR, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and order of the High Court.

directions: The impugned judgment and order of the High Court dated 16.10.2023 in application under Section 482 CrPC is set-aside.
The application under Section 482 of CrPC shall accordingly stand allowed.

The FIR No.272 of 2019 dated 29.09.2019 registered with Police Station South Rohini, Delhi under Sections 376(2)(n) and 506 of the IPC, charge-sheet dated 22.11.2019 filed in the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate, Rohini, Delhi and the trial pending in the Court of ASJ, Rohini, Delhi shall accordingly stand quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the FIR lodged against the appellant under Sections 376(2)(n) and 506 IPC should be quashed.

facts: The appellant and the complainant met in 2017 and began a relationship, meeting multiple times over the next two years.
The complainant alleged that in January 2019, the appellant began a forceful sexual relationship with her and threatened her.
The appellant later refused to marry the complainant and got married to someone else in 2019.
The complainant filed the FIR in September 2019, after the appellant's marriage.
The Court noted inconsistencies in the complainant's statements regarding the timeline of the alleged forceful acts (FIR vs. MLC report vs. Section 164 statement).
law: To determine if an FIR should be quashed, the court must assess whether, assuming all allegations are true, the essential ingredients of the alleged offenses are present.

For an offense under Section 376(2)(n) IPC (rape on a false promise of marriage), it must be shown that the promise of marriage was made at the outset of the relationship and was the sole reason the complainant engaged in the sexual relationship.
A mere breakup of a relationship does not automatically constitute an offense under Section 376 IPC.
application: The Court reviewed the FIR and the complainant's statement and found no indication that a promise of marriage was made at the beginning of their relationship in 2017.
It concluded that the sexual relationship was not solely based on an assurance of marriage from the appellant.
The Court observed that the relationship appeared to be consensual and cordial, noting that the complainant continued to meet the appellant even after the alleged forceful acts began.
The complaint was filed only after the appellant married someone else, suggesting it was motivated by the breakup rather than a non-consensual relationship.
Based on the cordial nature of their interactions and the timing of the complaint, the Court also found that the ingredients for criminal intimidation under Section 506 IPC were not met.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court was wrong to conclude there was no consent and had dismissed the quashing petition on a "completely misconceived basis."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the crucial ingredients for the offenses under Sections 376(2)(n) and 506 IPC were absent. Finding that continuing the prosecution would be an abuse of the court's process, it allowed the appeal and quashed the FIR.

issue.issue_text: Whether, assuming all the allegations in the FIR are correct, an offence punishable under Sections 376 and 506 IPC is made out.

facts: The appellant and the complainant met in 2017 and established a relationship, meeting multiple times until 2019.
The complainant alleged that the appellant had a forceful sexual relationship with her and threatened her.
Despite the alleged forceful act, the complainant continued to meet the appellant and did not file a criminal complaint during that period.
The complainant filed the FIR in 2019 only after the appellant got married.
The High Court had previously dismissed the appellant's petition to quash the FIR, finding the allegations sufficient to constitute the offenses.
law: The issue is whether the allegations in the FIR, taken at face value, constitute an offense under Section 376(2)(n) (repeated rape on the same woman) and Section 506 (criminal intimidation) of the IPC.
The court can exercise its power under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash proceedings to prevent an abuse of the court's process.
application: The Court analyzed the FIR and the complainant's statement and found no indication that a promise of marriage was made at the beginning of their relationship in 2017.
It concluded that the sexual relationship could not have been based solely on an assurance of marriage from the appellant.
The Court observed that the relationship between the parties was cordial and consensual in nature.
The fact that the complainant continued to meet the appellant after the alleged forceful act and only filed the complaint after his marriage indicated a consensual relationship, not sexual assault.

Based on these circumstances, the Court determined that the essential ingredients for the offenses of both rape under Section 376(2)(n) and criminal intimidation under Section 506 were not established.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that, even assuming all allegations in the FIR are correct, the essential ingredients of the offenses under Sections 376 and 506 IPC were not made out. It found the relationship was consensual and held that the High Court erred in not quashing the FIR, as continuing the prosecution would be an abuse of the court's process.

issue.issue_text: Whether the relationship between the parties was consensual in nature.

facts: The appellant and the complainant met in 2017 and were in a relationship until 2019.
They met multiple times at various places, including their respective houses.
The complainant alleged a forceful sexual act in January 2019 but continued to meet the appellant afterward and did not file a complaint at that time.
The court found it improbable that the appellant would know the complainant's address unless she had voluntarily provided it.
At one point, both parties intended to marry each other, but the plan did not materialize.
The appellant married someone else in 2019, and the complainant filed the FIR shortly after. The complainant later married someone else in 2020.
law: A relationship that begins consensually between two consenting adults cannot be given a criminal nature simply because it does not result in marriage.
For an offence of rape based on a promise to marry, there must be an indication that the promise was made at the outset of the relationship and was the sole reason for the complainant's consent.
Continuing a prosecution where the relationship was consensual amounts to a gross abuse of the process of law.
application: The Supreme Court found it "inconceivable" that the complainant would maintain a prolonged association and physical relationship with the appellant without her voluntary consent.
The court inferred that the complainant's continued meetings with the appellant after the alleged forceful act contradicted her claim of non-consent.
The court noted that both parties were educated adults who were in a cordial relationship with an intention to marry, which points towards a consensual arrangement.
The timing of the FIR, filed after the appellant's marriage, suggested to the court that the complaint was a result of the relationship ending, not a lack of consent from the beginning.

A review of the FIR and the complainant's statement showed no indication that a promise of marriage was made at the start of their relationship in 2017. Therefore, the court concluded that she did not engage in the sexual relationship solely because of such an assurance.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the relationship between the parties was consensual in nature. It held that a mere breakup of a consensual relationship cannot be the basis for criminal proceedings, and therefore, quashed the FIR and chargesheet against the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the FIR lodged against the appellant under Sections 376(2)(n) and 506 IPC should be quashed.
appellant_arguments: The appellant filed a petition to quash the FIR lodged against them.
respondent_arguments: The learned ASG argued that the High Court was justified in dismissing the quashing petition and that the appeal should also be dismissed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether, assuming all the allegations in the FIR are correct, an offence punishable under Sections 376 and 506 IPC is made out.
appellant_arguments: It can be inferred that the appellant argued that the allegations in the FIR, even if taken at face value, do not constitute a criminal offense under Sections 376 and 506 IPC.
respondent_arguments: It can be inferred that the respondent argued that the allegations in the FIR were sufficient to constitute an offense under the charged sections.

appellant_arguments: It can be inferred that the appellant argued the relationship was consensual, a point supported by the fact that both the appellant and the complainant subsequently married other people in 2019 and 2020, respectively.
respondent_arguments: It can be inferred that the respondent argued the relationship was not consensual, which formed the basis of the FIR for rape.

cases.case_name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
cases.principle: Cited for the established guidelines and categories of cases where the High Court can exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of the process of court.

cases.case_name: XXXX v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: Relied upon for the legal distinction between a mere 'breach of promise' to marry and a 'false promise to marry' which is false from its inception, where only the latter can vitiate consent and constitute the offence of rape.

cases.case_name: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: Cited for the principle that to establish the offence of rape on the basis of a false promise to marry, it must be proven that the promise was false from the very beginning and was the direct basis for the woman's consent to the sexual act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To establish that consent for a sexual act was vitiated by a 'misconception of fact' arising from a promise to marry, two propositions must be established: the promise of marriage must have been a false promise given in bad faith with no intention of being adhered to at the time it was given, and the false promise itself must bear a direct nexus to the woman’s decision to engage in the sexual act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The facts as they stand, which are not in dispute, indicate that the ingredients of the offence under Sections 376 (2)(n) or 506 IPC are not established in the instant case. The High Court erred in concluding that there was no consent on the part of the complainant and therefore she was a victim of sexual assault over a period of time and therefore, proceeded to dismiss the application under Section 482 CrPC on a completely misconceived basis.
legal_tests_applied: The power to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the CrPC can be exercised 'Where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.'

The power to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the CrPC can be exercised 'Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge.'”
policy_considerations: What was a consensual relationship between the parties at the initial stages cannot be given a colour of criminality when the said relationship does not fructify into a marital relationship.

The continuation of the prosecution in the present case would amount to a gross abuse of the process of law, particularly as both parties are now married to someone else and have moved on in their respective lives.
The power available under Section 482 CrPC should be exercised to prevent abuse of the court’s process by continuing the prosecution in such cases.
